metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Billings County, ND
metaDescription: Billings County heirs of old Badlands ranch homesteads: get a clear, no-pressure look at what your mineral interest near Medora is worth today.
heroLead: Billings County is Badlands country before it is oil country, and most of the mineral interests here still trace back to a ranch homestead patent nobody in the family has stood on in decades.
intro: Medora sits in the middle of Billings County looking more like a tourist town than an oil county, and in a lot of ways it is. Population here has stayed under a thousand for generations, the Little Missouri National Grasslands checkerboards federal and private land across most of the map, and the ranches that got patented in the homestead era were often thousands of acres, not the quarter-sections you see further east. When those ranch families split minerals among children and grandchildren, the fractions got small fast, and a lot of that ownership drifted out of state as the next generation moved to Bismarck, Minneapolis, or further.

We hear from Billings County owners who inherited a mineral interest through a great-aunt's estate and have no idea whether it sits under producing acreage or open grassland. Both situations are common here, and the honest answer starts with pulling the actual record, not guessing from the county name.

sections.heading: The Badlands Ranch Country Behind the Numbers
paragraphs: Most Billings County mineral tracts were carved out of large cattle-ranch patents rather than the tighter farm sections common in the eastern part of the state. That history matters for valuation because a single original ranch tract, once divided among heirs across three or four generations, can leave a present-day owner holding a fraction so small it barely shows up on a division order line. Knowing the original patent size helps explain why your percentage looks the way it does.

Billings County sits on the flank of the Bakken and Three Forks trend rather than its core, so activity has always been sparser and more dependent on commodity price cycles than counties closer to Watford City or Williston. That is not a reason to assume an interest is worthless, only a reason to check current status rather than rely on family memory of what the land was doing forty years ago.

sections.heading: Split Estate and the Checkerboard Around Medora
paragraphs: A lot of surface here belongs to the National Grasslands while minerals underneath stayed private, and adjoining private tracts can have entirely different lease histories depending on how the original homestead sat relative to federal sections. Confirming which pattern applies to your specific tract is a first step before anyone can give you a useful number.

Because so much of the county is federal surface, oil and gas activity depends heavily on how spacing units are drawn across the checkerboard, and a unit boundary can include or exclude your tract based on a survey line that has nothing to do with family history.

sections.heading: What a Billings County Royalty Check Usually Looks Like
paragraphs: Where wells exist, statements tend to be simple compared to core Bakken counties, often a single well or a small unit rather than the multi-well stacked-lateral spacing you see near Watford City. That simplicity cuts both ways: less to reconcile on the statement, but also less production spread across the interest if a well goes into decline.

Owners considering a sale here should weigh a lump-sum offer against the flank-county reality that new drilling is less certain than in core counties, and that a long stretch of low or no activity is common and does not necessarily mean the minerals stopped being worth anything.

sections.heading: Getting Your Interest Confirmed at the Courthouse in Medora
paragraphs: The Billings County Recorder's office in Medora holds the deed and probate chain for most tracts, but because the county is small and rural, older records sometimes require a courthouse visit or a title search rather than a quick online pull. If your family's documentation stops at a grandparent's will, that gap is exactly what a title search closes before any offer can be made specific to your acres.
We walk owners through exactly what to request from the recorder and how to read what comes back, at no cost, whether or not you decide to sell.

faqs.question: How do I know if my Billings County minerals are under a producing unit?
faqs.answer: Start with the Recorder's office in Medora for your legal description, then check that description against the North Dakota Industrial Commission's spacing unit records. We can walk you through both if you send us what you have.

faqs.question: Is Billings County part of the core Bakken?
faqs.answer: No, it sits on the flank, southwest of the McKenzie/Mountrail core. Activity has historically been lighter and more cycle-dependent, which affects both lease terms and how offers are typically priced.

faqs.question: My family's ranch was thousands of acres. Why is my mineral fraction so small?
faqs.answer: Large original homestead tracts divided across generations of heirs shrink individual fractions quickly. A great-grandparent's whole section can end up split into dozens of small interests by the time it reaches your generation.

faqs.question: Does federal grassland surface affect my private mineral rights?
faqs.answer: Not directly, since minerals and surface can be owned separately, but the checkerboard pattern does affect how spacing units and access roads get drawn, which affects whether your tract ends up inside a producing unit.

faqs.question: What if I only have an old probate document, not a current deed?
faqs.answer: That is common in Billings County estates. A title search can usually trace ownership forward from probate to the present, and we cover that cost as part of evaluating your interest.
